title: O13 and O14 (25 A) are reserved for the swap engine's ECU/injectors and…
body: **D-007 — O13 and O14 (25 A) are reserved for the swap engine's ECU/injectors and cooling fan**, wired to the engine leg and capped at the bulkhead (L1-P 2, L1-P 3). Three 16 AWG sensor spares (L1-S2 4–6) and the CAN2 drop (L1-S1 9/10, with the bus's far-end 120 Ω terminator across it) are capped in the same place.

system: What the electrical build reserves for the swap
title: The engine leg (L1) is built to be cut off at the firewall grommet and…
body:
**D-211(d) — The engine leg (L1) is built to be cut off at the firewall grommet and rebuilt from scratch at the swap.** It carries only what the 12A on the mounts needs today — no stubs to nothing, no connectors marking where something used to be. The reservations above are the only exceptions. Everything else about the new engine's wiring — ECU, sensors, fans, a PMU-driven A/C clutch and pressure transducer — is designed here, around whatever the engine is.

**D-211 — The 12A's A/C system comes out and cooling returns with the new engine.** The compressor, bracket, condenser and hoses are boxed and kept (FB A/C hardware is scarce). The new system is a new compressor on the new engine, a PMU-driven clutch and a pressure transducer — not the 1982 relay chain.

title: The PMU's fuel-pump and start-relay rules gain their rpm terms once rpm…
body: **D-183 — The PMU's fuel-pump and start-relay rules gain their rpm terms once rpm is on CAN2.** The ICU publishes it on `0x200` from the first drive (electrical D-259); the ECU's own arrives on `0x500+` at the swap. Either is a *secondary*, fail-open term — the primary gate is the hardwired oil-pressure node on A7 (electrical D-249 / D-251).

body:
**D-113 — The rear disc conversion and the rear axle are still planned.** The July 2026 drum overhaul was an interim so the car could be driven; the intent is a thoroughly sorted rear axle and engine that then last.

**Electrical D-261 / D-262 — the 12A's senders stay and are read in place; every ICU sensor channel is jumper-and-config, the PMU's A7 takes a sender or a 0–5 V transducer.** What the new engine must deliver to those inputs is the hand-over table in [`README.md`](README.md).

system: What the electrical build reserves for the swap
title: The A/C clutch is a DCU-switched comfort load; the PMU is not opened for it
body:
**D-324 — The A/C clutch is a DCU-switched comfort load; the PMU is not opened for it.** Camden's call, 2026-09-11, answering `02.01`: "I want all A/C comfort controls together manged by the dcu no pmu tear down and change up."

D-211 said "a PMU-driven clutch and a pressure transducer", but every one of the PMU's 22 outputs is allocated — O13 and O14 are this project's ECU and cooling fan. Rather than re-allocate a channel and reopen a 39-way connector that D-004 assembles once, the clutch joins the comfort group where the rest of the A/C controls already are.

**The arrangement.** The clutch is a relay whose coil the **DCU** switches on one of its seven comfort FETs (luxury `SN16`, parts under luxury `V-083`), contact fed from the luxury package's **O15 comfort block**. The pressure transducer goes to a **DCU input**. The A/C toggle is already drawn on the control panel (luxury D-210). No PMU output, no harness change, and the clutch feed runs from the O15 block into the rebuilt engine leg at the swap — which suits D-271, since the leg is built from scratch then anyway.

**What this forecloses, accepted.** The clutch cannot engage with the DCU down. That is the correct trade for a comfort load: it matches D-081's principle that modules add capability to a finished car and are never a dependency for it starting, running or being legal.

system: What the electrical build reserves for the swap
title: The swap ECU is a dash node; no CAN and no ECU in the engine bay
body:
**D-325 — The swap ECU is a dash node; no CAN and no ECU in the engine bay.** Camden's call, 2026-09-11, inside `00.04`: "I do not want the ecu in the engine bay … I want as stripped clean of an engine bay as possible and do not want to put anything there unless there is no way to avoid it. The ECU will also be a dash node localized with all the other computers and more intricate wiring, then only the small branches travel everywhere."

The electrical build's counterpart is **D-318**. The consequence here is that `HO03` changes shape: CAN2 no longer reaches the bay, `L1-S1 9` and `10` return to sealing plugs, and the far-end 120 Ω terminator moves to the dash node. A future ECU joins the bus **at the dash**, at 0x500+ as luxury's CAN map already allocates, and what leaves the dash for the engine is only the sensor and actuator branches the rebuilt leg pins.

**What this asks of the swap.** The ECU must be one that tolerates a cabin mounting and a longer sensor harness — which is the normal case for every ECU worth fitting, and is how the factory mounted its own control units. Long runs to crank and cam sensors are shielded, as `L1-S1 6` already is for the tach. Nothing about this reserves less: O13 and O14 stay the ECU and fan channels (D-007), and the leg still ends at the firewall grommet (D-211).

title: The swap engine is a light, aluminum-block 5.3 LS - L33 first, then LM4, then an LH6 or LC9 with AFM deleted; an iron LM7 is the fallback
body:
**D-393 — The swap engine is a light, aluminum-block 5.3 LS.** The order of preference:
1. **L33:** aluminum, no AFM.
2. **LM4:** aluminum, no AFM.
3. **LH6 or LC9:** aluminum, with AFM deleted.

An iron LM7 is the fallback if no aluminum engine can be had. Camden's call, 2026-09-23.

**His words.** "can you find me a specific pic an pull junk yard near Fort Collins that is guaranteed to have one of the light iron blocks that id want, write all this in the engine swap project"

**Reading taken.** The light 5.3 blocks are aluminum; the iron ones (LM7, LMG, LY5, LR4) are the heavy ones, about 80 lb more dressed. "Light" is what he wants, so the target is aluminum. If he meant iron, the target is the LM7 (option OP05) and the sightings are searched again for code T.

**What the research found.** It is recorded in the new tables (`options`, `yards`, `sightings`):
- **Aluminum 5.3s:** common in 2007–2013 trucks as the LC9, less so as the LH6. The L33 (2005–07 extended-cab 1500s) and the LM4 are uncommon.
- **What a U-pull engine costs:** about $260–276 plus a $57–75 core near Denver.
- **The transmission:** the CD009 costs about $1,650–2,150 used and delivered. The Sikky adapter ($1,765) needs no bellhousing cutting.
- **Kits:** no bolt-in LS kit exists for the FB.
- **The CD009 in an FB:** no documented build was found, so it is the plan's biggest unknown (J3, J4).
- **The rear axle:** the stock FB axle will not take LS torque (D-113 already plans a new one).

**What "guaranteed" can honestly mean.** No yard can guarantee an engine. On 2026-09-23, 15 aluminum 5.3 donors were confirmed on the lot by the VIN's 8th digit, all in the Denver metro, about 60–65 miles away: two LH6 and thirteen LC9. There were none in Fort Collins, Greeley, Loveland or Cheyenne; those yards publish no inventory. No L33 was confirmed anywhere. One possible L33 is at Littleton (J2). A listing means the car is on the lot, not that its engine is still in it, so J1 calls ahead with the VIN.

**In the data.**
- `_tables` and `_schema`: `options`, `yards` and `sightings` are new.
- `options`: OP01–OP50.
- `yards`: YD01–YD09.
- `sightings`: SG01–SG16.
- `work`: J1–J5.

title: The new engine leg is designed backwards from every LS and CD009 part: pins, bay joins, conductors that cross, dash ends - and it needs about 55-65 small conductors against the 24 small cavities today
body:
**D-394 — The swap's new engine leg is designed backwards from every LS and CD009 part.** For each part the design records:
1. its pins;
2. what is joined in the bay;
3. how many conductors cross into the leg;
4. where each lands at the dash.

The result: the power side fits the leg's power plug L1-P as it is, and the signal side needs 54–68 conductors against the 24 signal cavities today. Camden's call, 2026-09-23.

**His words.** "help me plan the electrical side of engine swap, we will be replacing the entire engine leg, specifically for this design work backwards, ignore the wiring we have and build the electrical system backwards from each Ls part/attachment, this schools then plug in to the same engine leg connecter at the dash post"

**The method.** `ls_devices` lists 26 parts on or around the engine. `ls_wires` gives 39 wire functions. For each function it records:
- how many wires there are at the device;
- what is spliced or grounded in the bay;
- how many conductors cross into the leg;
- the Deutsch contact size needed;
- the dash end, gauge, current, twist or shield group, and whether it is optional.

The leg's size is a query over `ls_wires`, never a typed number (R2).

**The rules the design follows.**
- **Bay joins:** feeds are spliced in the bay (one 12 AWG feed to eight injectors, one to eight coils). Power grounds stay in the bay, at the head studs. Sensor grounds and 5 V references are spliced in the bay but go back to the ECU, never to chassis.
- **Shields:** crank, cam and knock are shielded, with the drain at the ECU end only.
- **Returns:** the reverse switch and the oil-temperature sender return to the dash, not the block. That keeps the cranking ground offset (risk review R3) and the fuel-sender lesson out of the readings.
- **Oil pressure:** one sensor and one wire, read by the PMU's A7 gate (D-249, HO04). The ECU and the ICU get it at the dash.

**What it found.**
- **Power fits L1-P as it is:**
  - coils on O12 (L1-P 1, the same cavity that feeds the 12A's coils);
  - injectors on O13 (L1-P 2);
  - the fan on O14 (L1-P 3);
  - the A/C clutch feed from the O15 comfort block in the spare L1-P 4.
- **Signals do not fit.** 54 required and 68 with every option, against 24 in L1-S1 and L1-S2. No ECU choice changes this. It contradicts handover row HO14 ("nothing at the dash node changes"). How the extra connects at the post is his call: block `02.02`.
- **HO08 is superseded for the ECU.** It says "no +5 V goes down the leg". That was written for the PMU's and ICU's sensors. The ECU's own 5 V has to go down the leg now that the ECU is at the dash (LW20).
- **Open until the parts are in hand:** every pin letter, and the generation-specific details (Gen III or Gen IV, D-393). They are `confirm` (R11, work K4).

**Still to decide.**
- **The ECU:** K1 researches it, then asks him in a block.
- **The emissions equipment:** K2 checks the rules, which settle the O2 sensors and the purge.
- **The cavity plan and grommet:** K3, after `02.02`.

**In the data.**
- `_tables` and `_schema`: `ls_devices` and `ls_wires` are new.
- `ls_devices`: LD01–LD26.
- `ls_wires`: LW01–LW39.
- `work`: K1–K4.
- `BLOCKS.md`: `02.02` is new.

title: The swap runs in nine stages: -01 design, 00 buy and retrieve, 01 breakdown, 02 polish, 03 paint, 04 rebuild, 05 car prep, 06 install, 07 fine-tune - and the first full plan fills them
body:
**D-395 — The swap runs in nine stages, and the first full plan fills them.**

| Stage | What happens in it |
|---|---|
| **-01 Design** | Every choice is made on paper before money is spent. |
| **00 Buy and retrieve** | The engine, the transmission and the parts. |
| **01 Breakdown** | Strip, inspect and measure on stands. |
| **02 Polish** | Degrease, derust, surface prep. |
| **03 Paint** | The engine, the brackets and the parts that show. |
| **04 Rebuild** | Reseal, the AFM delete, service parts, assembly, pre-lube. |
| **05 Car prep** | The 12A out, then the bay, tunnel, mounts, fuel, cooling, exhaust, axle, pedals and the new leg. |
| **06 Install** | In the car, connected, fluids, first start. |
| **07 Fine-tune** | The tune, the shakedown, emissions, the record. |

Camden's call, 2026-09-23.

**His words.** "Now what prep can I do the the engine out of the car aka clean paint reaseal se fluid derust make a stage  stage -02-design, -01-buy-retrieve, 00-breakdown, 01-polish, 02-paint, 03-rebuild, 04-car-prep, 05-install, 06-fine-tune, (add one to each number) then please fill in a full start of a plan for this structure and project"

**Reading taken.** "Add one to each number" is applied literally, so -02 becomes -01 and 06 becomes 07. The stages are values of `work.stage` with their titles in `stage_title`, so the project's TODO groups by them. No folders were made, because the plan is rows. If he meant a different numbering (01–09) or folders like the electrical project's, it is a rename.

**The plan: 63 new rows, each gated on what it truly waits for.**
- **-01 Design:** DS01–DS11. They cover the accessory drive, the FB-clearance oil pan, headers, cooling against O14's 25 A, the returnless fuel system, the clutch pedal and hydraulics (the car is an automatic today), mounts and crossmember, the rear axle (D-113), springs, and a derived budget. DS11 is his design freeze. The rows already in the project join this stage: K1 the ECU, K2 emissions, K3 the cavity plan, J3 and J4 the tunnel, H-001 the alternator.
- **00 Buy and retrieve:** BR01–BR06. They cover stands and tools, the yard pull (with the list of what to take), the CD009 after the tunnel is measured and the design frozen, the adapter kit and clutch, the rebuild parts from the breakdown's findings, and the car-prep parts. J1, J2 and J5 join this stage.
- **01 Breakdown:** BD01–BD08. They record the numbers, then read the fluids, strip and label, take the heads off where the AFM delete needs it, and inspect the pan and bearings. The CD009 is checked on its stand. The breakdown ends with his ruling on the rebuild scope, and K4 (read the real pin letters) joins it.
- **02 Polish:** PO01–PO04. Degrease with every opening plugged, derust the steel, and mask every machined face before paint.
- **03 Paint:** PA01–PA03. The colours are his call, because the engine and the bay are seen together. Then high-temperature enamel, and the small parts.
- **04 Rebuild:** RB01–RB08. The AFM delete (LH6 / LC9 only), timing and oil pump, heads on new single-use bolts, rear main and the swap pan, water pump, sensors and injectors, gaskets, the adapter, flywheel, clutch and CD009, then pre-lube.
- **05 Car prep:** CP01–CP10. The 12A and the automatic out (the old leg is cut here, D-211), then:
  - a clean bay (D-325), tunnel work and mounts;
  - the pedal box, fuel, cooling, axle and driveshaft;
  - the new engine leg and the ECU at the dash;
  - springs.
- **06 Install:** IN01–IN06. In the car, plumbing, electrical, fluids, then the checks before the first start: oil pressure, fuel pressure, crank and cam signals. Then the first start.
- **07 Fine-tune:** TU01–TU07. The base tune, then CAN integration: the ICU and the PMU's rpm terms (D-183), and the soft fuses set from measured currents. Then road tests with a charging check, a dyno tune, alignment, and emissions and registration. Last, the as-built goes into 00-CAR (CLAUDE.md §6.6).

**Rules the plan keeps.**
- **Nothing past the engine is bought before the design freeze (DS11).** It is the same discipline as the electrical project.
- **The breakdown's measurements set the rebuild scope, not the plan (R11).** Worn bores or bad bearings turn a reseal into a rebuild.
- **The donor harness is kept intact** as the reference for the new leg's pin letters.

title: The swap's engine leg stays DT at the dash post: L1-P as today, the signal side grows to six DT06-12S (72 cavities)
body:
**The swap's engine leg stays on Deutsch DT at the dash post: L1-P (DTP 4-way) is unchanged, and the signal side grows from two DT06-12S plugs (L1-S1, L1-S2) to six (72 cavities, room for every option in `ls_wires`). Same contacts, same crimper (P038) and removal tools as every other leg. The dash-node carrier panels are laid out now with room for the four extra DT04-12P receptacles beside L1-S1 and L1-S2.**

**His answer (block 02.12, desktop, 2026-09-27):** option (a) — "**More of the same connector.** L1-P stays as it is, and the signal side grows from two 12-way DT plugs to five (60 cavities) or six (72, room for every option). Same contacts, same crimper (P038) and removal tools already on the cart, same method as every other leg. Costs a few more DT housing pairs (confirm price), room on the dash post for 3–4 more receptacles (measured at M-1), and a bigger firewall grommet." He typed no words.

**Reading.** Option (a) left five or six plugs open; the recommendation was "(a) with six signal plugs". Six is the reading that keeps the most open (every optional conductor — MAF, narrowband O2s, VVT, purge, oil temperature, neutral switch — keeps a cavity) and the difference is one DT housing pair, so it is taken. If K3's cavity plan fills fewer than 60 cavities, the sixth pair is simply not bought; that is a parts-round detail, not a new ruling.

**Why.** 54 signal conductors are required and 68 with every option (D-394, `ls_wires`) against 24 cavities in L1-S1 and L1-S2. No ECU choice changes this. DT needs no new tooling and matches every other leg.

**What changes.**
- Handover HO14 no longer says "nothing at the dash node changes": the 39-way PMU pins and the dash-node conductors stay the fixed interface, but four more DT04-12P receptacles join L1-S1 and L1-S2 at the post at the swap. Today's 12A leg is still built alone and cut at the grommet (D-211(d)); nothing is bought now.
- Electrical E13 (dash node layout) leaves panel room for four more DT04-12P receptacles next to L1-S1 / L1-S2, so the swap does not re-cut a panel. Whether that room exists is still measured at M-1 (C1); if it does not, that is a new block, and (b) (one high-density plug) is the fallback the block named.
- Engine K3 (cavity plan and grommet size) is released: its gate was this block. It assigns `ls_wires` crossing conductors to L1-P and six 12-way signal plugs, and sizes the bigger firewall grommet.

title: The swap leg's cavity plan: every crossing conductor to a cavity in L1-P and L1-S1 to L1-S6 by noise class; the grommet is chosen for a 25 mm bundle
body:
**The swap leg's cavity plan is table `ls_cavities`: every crossing conductor in `ls_wires` has one cavity in L1-P or the six DT06-12S signal plugs L1-S1 to L1-S6 (D-443), grouped by noise class; the firewall grommet must pass a bundle of about 17 mm of conductors, so it is chosen for a 25 mm bundle (confirm at CP09).**

Work K3, released by D-443 (block 02.12). Small under §3: paper, rows only, nothing bought or cut; arithmetic and the standing rules settle it.

**The groups** (one noise class per housing, drivers never sharing a plug with a sensor signal):
- **L1-P** (power, unchanged): 1 coil feed O12, 2 injector feed O13, 3 fan O14, 4 A/C clutch from the O15 block — as D-394 and today's leg.
- **L1-S1 drivers**: injector drivers 1-8, the throttle motor pair, the start relay K9 coil, purge.
- **L1-S2 drivers**: coil triggers 1-8, the two ignition reference grounds with them, the VVT pair.
- **L1-S3 shielded timing**: crank (signal, supply, ground, drain), cam (the same), road speed; 11-12 spare.
- **L1-S4 low-level analog**: the four knock conductors and their drain, the two throttle positions with the throttle's own 5 V and ground, the neutral switch pair; 12 spare.
- **L1-S5 analog sensors**: MAP, IAT, coolant, oil pressure, the shared 5 V and two sensor grounds, MAF, the O2 signals and lows.
- **L1-S6 body and slow lines**: alternator excitation and lamp sense, A/C pressure (3), reverse pair, oil temperature pair, the O2 heater drivers (slow PWM, kept off the sensor plugs); 12 spare.

Every shield drain is grounded at the ECU end only (K3's rule, electrical `emc-routing`). 72 cavities, 68 used with every option kept, 54 required; the 14 optional conductors keep their cavities, so dropping an option later (K2 decides O2 and purge) leaves a sealing plug and moves nothing. A cross-check: `select wire, count(*) from ls_cavities group by wire` equals each row's `crosses`.

**Grommet.** Crossing conductors by gauge (a query over `ls_wires`): 3 × 12 AWG, 1 × 14, 1 × 16, 27 × 18, 40 × 20. With TXL outside diameters (12: 2.46, 14: 2.08, 16: 1.73, 18: 1.52, 20: 1.37 mm — catalogue class figures, confirm against the wire bought) the sum of squared diameters is about 163 mm², a round bundle at 60 % fill of about 16.5 mm. The wideband gauge's own sensor lead passes the same grommet (LD12, D-244) and the shielded groups add jackets, so the grommet is chosen for a 25 mm bundle; the firewall hole follows that grommet's datasheet at CP09. The dash-end housings are pinned after the bundle has passed the grommet, so no plug has to fit through the hole.

**Not done here.** The dash side (ECU pins to these receptacles) waits on the ECU choice (K1); new work row K5 carries it.

title: The swap's alternator is rated 160 A or more for about 160 A of running load, its set-point held at or under 14.6 V by the ECU
body:
**The swap's alternator is sized for about 160 A of running load with every load on: it must be rated 160 A or more (a GM truck-case unit, not the F-body 105 A class), and its regulator set-point must stay at or under the Ionic's 14.6 V ceiling (00-CAR SP-231), commanded by the ECU through the alternator control line (LW29).**

Work H-001, from Camden's note on luxury D-391: "worth noting in enine swap that alternator needs to be beefy". Small under §3: arithmetic over rows already in the record; which alternator and bracket are bought stays with DS01's accessory-drive choice, which now has this floor.

**The sum** (design currents at 13.5 V; measured where the record has it):
- Car, from electrical `loads`: headlights high 8.9 (halogen today; LED at luxury S7 lowers it), tail and park 5.4 measured, brake lamps 7.0 measured, interior 2.5, wiper high 5.5, blower on high 18, rear defog 13, accessory bus 10 — 70.3 A.
- Comfort, from electrical D-382 and V-101: seat heat 5 A × 2 (heat and cool interlocked per seat, so heat is the larger), mirror heat 5 (its fuse, a bound, confirm), DCU and PMU about 1 — 16 A.
- Engine, from `ls_wires.amps`: injectors 9, coils 12, fan 25 (O14's limit), A/C clutch 4, throttle motor 5, O2 heaters 3, VVT 1.5, purge 0.5; plus the in-tank pump about 12.2 A at 58 psi (the Phantom 340 candidate, electrical V-040, confirm) and the ECU about 1 (confirm) — 73.2 A.

Everything at once is about 160 A. A cold wet night (no fan, brakes off) is about 128 A; a hot night in traffic with the fan, A/C and seat cooling instead of heat and defog is about 140 A. An alternator gives roughly half to two-thirds of its rating at hot idle (class figure, confirm on the unit's curve), so a 160 A unit covers the realistic cases at speed and the LiFePO4 battery carries the idle shortfall; the 12A's 55 A class alternator (electrical V-002) and a 105 A F-body unit do not.

**The regulator.** An LS alternator's set-point is commanded (Gen III: the L / field lines; Gen IV trucks: a PWM command). The ECU chosen at K1 must drive LW29 so the set-point holds at or under 14.6 V; an uncommanded unit's default voltage is confirmed on the bench before it is fitted.

**In the data.** DS01's note carries the 160 A floor; K1's note adds alternator control to what each ECU must offer.

title: Engine computer: ECUMaster EMU PRO
body:
**The LS swap is designed around the ECUMaster EMU PRO (option OP60).**

His answer to block 02.13: option (a), no words added. Option (a) in full: "ECUMaster EMU PRO, about $1,800-2,400 (confirm): the same maker and the same laptop software family as the power unit (PMU), sends any CAN message we define, reads either crank signal so any engine on the list works, built to take our own harness through the dash post. Forecloses nothing; the dearest option but one."

Reasoning: it matches the recommendation; it keeps the engine hunt open to both crank generations in D-393's list, gives our own CAN frames at 0x500+ without a translator, and keeps one software family with the PMU.

Consequences: K1 (ECU research) and K5 (pinning the leg at the dash) are no longer waiting on 02.13 and go to the plan playbook. The price, output count, built-in wideband and the alternator set-point output for LW29 (D-445) stay `confirm` until checked, before anything is bought (BR06). DS10 carries the ECU line at OP60's range; DS11 no longer waits on this.

title: Fuel pump: Aeromotive Phantom 340 in-tank
body:
**The LS swap's fuel pump is the Aeromotive Phantom 340, in the tank.**

His answer to block 02.14: option (a), no words added. Option (a) in full: "Aeromotive Phantom 340, the candidate already named in HO12: a universal in-tank pump with its own baffle, fitted through a hole cut in the top of the existing tank. About 12.2 A, leaving O5 about half its 25 A spare. Carries a stock 5.3 easily and leaves room for a lot more power later. The tank is cut, and that cannot be undone."

Reasoning: it matches the recommendation; the margin for later power outweighs the 3 A over option (b). The tank cut is irreversible, so DS12 (measuring the tank top first) must be done before any cutting; the choice authorises the design, not the cut.

Consequences: DS05's parts list is built on the Phantom 340; the fuel pump's soft fuse on O5 is sized to about 12.2 A (D-173) at 58 psi (V-040); DS10 carries the pump line; CP06 (fuel work) is designed for a cut tank. Prices stay `confirm` until checked (BR06). DS05 and DS12 no longer wait on 02.14.

title: The swap's fuel system: Phantom 340 in the tank, a 58 psi filter-regulator by the tank, one 3/8 in feed to the rail; its parts are the new parts table
body:
**The swap's fuel system is the Phantom 340 in the tank feeding a 58 psi filter-regulator mounted by the tank, one 3/8 in (-6) feed forward to the rail and a short return back into the tank; its parts are rows FP01-FP06 in the new table `parts`, every part number, price and length `confirm`.**

Work DS05, released by D-447 (block 02.14). Small under §3: paper and rows only. The layout (LS returnless at 58 psi, a Corvette-style filter-regulator, one feed line) was already settled in DS05's note; the pump is his ruling; nothing is bought until the freeze (DS11) and BR06.

**The layout.** Pump in the tank (FP01) → filter-regulator by the tank (FP02), its return short into the pump's top plate or the tank's existing return, whichever the tank measurement (DS12) finds → one feed forward along the floor pan (FP03, clamped by FP06) → the rail's 3/8 in quick-connect (FP05). The Weber's Carter P4070, the Holley regulator and the second line forward go out at CP01; the old return line forward is capped or kept as a spare.

**Why a table.** The swap had no home for a part that is not an option; DS10 is the budget "over options, parts and this plan", so `parts` is declared here (system, item, spec, qty, unit, usd_low, usd_high, work, note) and DS10's total is a sum over it, never typed.

**Lengths.** The feed is bought at 1.5 × the route; the route is unmeasured, about 4.5 m tank to rail on the FB's 2420 mm wheelbase (confirm), so 7 m is listed and re-set from the tape at CP06.

**The soft fuse.** O5's soft fuse is set at about 140 % of the pump's measured draw (D-173, V-040): on the 12.2 A estimate that is about 17 A, well inside O5's 25 A; the number is set from the installed pump's measurement at CP06/TU02, not from this estimate.

**Not done here.** The tank cut waits on DS12. The EVAP vent and purge follow K2.

title: The swap leg's cavity plan corrected: today's functions keep today's cavities in L1-S1 and L1-S2, unused ones are reserved, the drivers take the new plugs; the cabin and dash wiring is declared
body:
**The swap leg's cavity plan is corrected: L1-S1 and L1-S2 are today's receptacles at the post, so every function that carries on keeps today's cavity, the cavities whose dash conductors the swap does not use are reserved and never pinned, and the injectors, coils, VVT and throttle motor take the new plugs L1-S3 and L1-S4. The cabin and dash wiring the swap adds - the ECU's own supply, grounds and ignition sense, the drive-by-wire pedal and the clutch switch into A4 - is declared in `ls_wires`. Supersedes D-444.**

Work K6, from the wiring review of 2026-09-28. Small under §3: paper, rows only, nothing bought, cut or wired; today's wiring is not touched, and the cavity facts come from electrical's own `cavities` and `node_conductors`.

**What was wrong.** D-444 filled L1-S1 and L1-S2 as if they were empty. They are not: their receptacles at the post are wired today (electrical `cavities`, `node_conductors` N19, N40, N41, N45-N50, N67, N68), and at the swap only the leg side is rebuilt (D-211, HO14). As planned, injector 1's driver would have landed on the K9 coil conductor, coil 1's trigger on the brake warning node N50 (a handbrake pull would have grounded it), injector 6 on the ICU's tach input, the K9 coil on the A4 ladder, and an ignition reference ground on L1-S2 9, which carries switched 12 V once its fuse is fitted. Nothing today is wrong; the swap would have been.

**The rule.** A cavity of L1-S1 or L1-S2 carries at the swap what it carries today, or a sealing plug. `ls_cavities` gains `state` (pinned or reserved) and `note`; a reserved row has no `wire` and names the dash conductor its receptacle carries.
- Kept, pinned as today: L1-S1 1 the K9 coil (LW30), L1-S1 2 the alternator excitation (LW29), L1-S1 4 oil pressure (LW16, the A7 gate and the ICU), L1-S2 1 the brake fluid switch (new LW41, LD27), L1-S2 7 reverse (LW37, the A5 ladder), L1-S2 8 the alternator lamp line (LW29).
- Reserved, a sealing plug in the swap leg: L1-S1 3 (water temperature gauge, IC01 - pinned only if a gauge sender is fitted, HO06), L1-S1 6 (tach, IC04 - no engine-bay source once the ECU fires the coils, HO05), L1-S1 11 (A4 - the clutch switch reaches N40 in the cabin, HO10), L1-S2 9 (the 12 V sensor supply, HO08), L1-S2 11 (the ICU's spare input IC17, HO09).
- The free cavities of L1-S1 and L1-S2 take slow lines: the ECU's coolant temperature and IAT, the throttle position group, the reverse return, the A/C pressure sensor, the alternator set-point command (new LW40), the oil temperature pair on L1-S2 10 and 12 (L1-S2 10 is the cavity D-264 kept for it).
- New plugs: L1-S3 injectors 1-8, the throttle motor pair and purge (one spare); L1-S4 coil triggers 1-8, the two reference grounds and the O2 heater drivers, which leave the sensor plug they shared in D-444; L1-S5 crank, cam and road speed, each shielded with its drain; L1-S6 knock, the O2 signals and lows, MAP, the 5 V reference and a sensor ground.

**Road speed has one route.** The CD009's VSS crosses L1 with the reverse and neutral switches from the same case (LW39), shielded whatever the sensor type, its drain (new LW48) at the ECU end like crank, cam and knock. The L4 tunnel pair (HO15) is spare at the swap.

**Declared, never through the leg** (`crosses` 0): the clutch switch with its 8.2 kOhm at the switch into N40 (LW42); the DBW pedal, two tracks each with its own 5 V and ground (LD28, LW43, LW44); the ECU itself (LD29) with its +12 V from O13 tapped at the dash node through its own fuse (LW45, D-007), its power grounds to the dash node's ground bus (LW46) and its ignition sense off the ignition switch's RUN output (LW47). Pin counts, gauges and fuse values come from the EMU PRO manual at K5 and stay confirm.

**Wire.** The leg is GXL, as the electrical build buys (D-212): 20 AWG GXL is about 1.7 mm over the insulation, inside the DT size-16 seal's 1.35-3.05 mm, where 20 AWG TXL (about 1.37 mm) sits at its floor (D-115; both figures confirm against the datasheets). The `ls_wires.awg` note says so.

**The grommet,** re-counted with GXL (catalogue class diameters, confirm: 12 AWG 3.0, 14 2.6, 16 2.2, 18 1.9, 20 1.7 mm): the 70 pinned conductors (3 x 12, 1 x 14, 1 x 16, 25 x 18, 40 x 20) square-sum to about 244 mm2, a 20.2 mm bundle at 60 % fill; with the five options waiting below, about 20.8 mm; with the wideband's own lead and the four shield jackets, about 24 mm. The grommet is chosen for a 28 mm bundle (D-444 said 25), confirm at CP09.

**What does not fit.** Six plugs hold 72 cavities; five are reserved and six keep today's functions, leaving 61 for 65 further conductors with every option: the MAF (LW24), the VVT pair (LW34) and the neutral switch pair (LW38) - the three options least likely to be wanted (speed density is the EMU PRO's own mode, VVT is only the 2010+ LC9, last in D-393's list, and the neutral switch may not exist on the CD009 bought) - have no cavity. D-443 chose six plugs as room for every option, so a seventh plug is his call; it is drafted as a block. Until then `select wire, count(*) from ls_cavities group by wire` equals each row's `crosses` except for those three.

**The coolant level sensor.** The 12A's radiator sensor (00-CAR PT292, confirmed on the car at 00-verify B26) leaves with the 12A radiator, and nothing in the swap replaces it. Whether the swap fits one is money and engine protection, drafted as a block; its natural home is the reserved L1-S2 11 into the ICU's spare input, which costs no cavity.

**Handover.** HO04-HO11 and HO15 are rewritten to say what each of today's cavities does at the swap.

title: The swap's alternator stays rated 160 A or more for about 163 A of load with F16 and F20; its set-point on its own ECU line; charge current and load dump at 160 A are K7; the pump is the Phantom 340 at about 12.2 A
body:
**The swap's alternator floor stands at 160 A, re-summed with the two O12-fed loads D-445 left out (the display's backlight on F16 and the wideband controller on F20): about 163 A with everything on. Its set-point is held at or under 14.6 V by the ECU's own command line, LW40, which is pinned in place of today's excitation if the unit bought is commanded. What the alternator may push into the LiFePO4 pack, and what a 160 A load dump does to the TVS, become work row K7. The fuel pump is the Phantom 340 at about 12.2 A, carried by O5, K13 and L4-P 2 as they are. Supersedes D-445.**

Work K6, from the wiring review of 2026-09-28. Small under §3: arithmetic over rows in the record; the floor does not move, so nothing bought changes.

**The sum.** D-445's 160 A, plus electrical F16 (the display's ignition feed through the ICU carrier, D-268; about 1.5 A, its fuse 5 A a bound, confirm) and F20 (the wideband controller, about 1.5 A running and more while its heater warms, its fuse 7.5 A a bound, confirm): about 163 A with every load on at once. The realistic cases move by the same 3 A, to about 131 A (cold wet night) and 143 A (hot traffic). A 160 A unit still covers both at speed, and the battery carries the everything-at-once case and the idle shortfall, as D-445 reasoned. One term is still open: the audio amplifier (D-449) has no row in electrical `loads` yet; its average draw is added when it is picked, and DS01 re-checks the floor then.

**The set-point.** D-445 named LW29 as the control line; LW29 is today's excitation and lamp pair, which keep their cavities (L1-S1 2, L1-S2 8). The ECU's command is its own conductor, LW40, on L1-S2 6. A commanded unit (a Gen IV style L terminal) takes LW40 and L1-S1 2 is a sealing plug; a unit with an excitation terminal keeps L1-S1 2 and its default set-point is checked at or under 14.6 V on the bench before it is fitted (00-CAR SP-231). Never both on one terminal.

**What a 160 A alternator brings that a 55 A one did not** (new K7, gated on DS01 and electrical W-330b):
- Charge current. With few loads on, a 160 A unit can push well over 100 A into a 40 Ah pack after a long crank - above 2C. If the S9H's BMS opens on over-current, that is the load dump W-330b's third question describes, at full alternator output. The pack's maximum continuous charge current is a fourth question for Ionic (proposed for electrical W-330b), and K7 caps the ECU's commanded current or set-point to it.
- Load dump. The PMU-feed TVS (electrical P136) was sized with the 12A's alternator in mind; the energy of a dump scales with the alternator's current. K7 checks P136 against a 160 A unit's dump (ISO 16750-2 test B, the unit's own figures), or names an alternator-side suppressor. The alternator's own cable and fuse at 160 A are electrical block 01.24.

**The fuel pump (HO12).** The Phantom 340 is chosen (D-447): about 12.2 A at 58 psi (electrical V-040, confirm on the bench). O5 (25 A) carries it with its soft fuse re-set to about 140 % of the measured draw, about 17 A (D-173); K13's contact (Song Chuan 871-1C-C, 40 A, electrical P003) and L4-P 2's 12 AWG carry it with room. HO12 says so, no longer "candidate".

title: At the swap the ECU owns the A/C clutch and the pressure sensor; the DCU only sends the request on CAN
body:
**At the swap the ECU owns the A/C: it switches the compressor clutch through a relay in the bay and reads the refrigerant pressure sensor on its own 5 V and sensor ground. The DCU's part is the request - one byte on its climate frame - and nothing on the DCU board changes.**

Camden answered block 02.15 in chat on 2026-10-12: "a". Option (a) as he was asked it: "The ECU owns the clutch and the pressure sensor; the DCU's A/C key becomes a CAN request. No DCU change." Not taken: (b) the DCU keeps both - its board already carries the clutch stage and the pressure input as unpopulated parts (electrical SN28 / SN29, about $16), which is cheaper than the block said, but two boards would then have to agree about the compressor and the ECU still needs the request for idle-up and the full-throttle cut.

**What it means at the swap.** The EMU PRO drives the clutch relay's coil from one of its outputs; the relay's contact feed comes from the O15 comfort block's spare position (fuses F29 position 6, the swap's to pin) through the engine leg (LW32, L1-P 4), as D-324 routed it - D-324's reason, no spare PMU output, still holds; what changes is who switches the relay. The pressure transducer wires to the ECU in the bay: its 5 V and sensor ground splice into LW20 / LW21 and its signal goes to an ECU analog input, so LW33 no longer crosses to the dash post and L1-S2 3 is free. The DCU sends its A/C request on 0x300 byte 4 (electrical can_fields), 1 when it wants the compressor - the panel sketch's rule, set temperature below outside air with the fan on, once he rules the sketch - and the ECU reads that frame as a CAN input (its setup at the swap, confirm). Until the swap the byte stays 0: there is no compressor (D-211).

**What stays on the DCU.** The clutch stage and the pressure input stay on the carrier as unpopulated footprints (electrical D-455's provision) and nothing is bought for them (P185, P186); the comfort fuse F29 stays 7.5 A. D-324's principle - the compressor is a comfort load that never gates the car starting or running - holds with the ECU owning it: the ECU cuts it at full throttle and the request is advisory.

**In the data.** Engine: handover HO13, ls_devices LD17 / LD18, ls_wires LW32 / LW33, ls_cavities L1-P 4 / L1-S2 3. Electrical: dcu_channels SN28 / SN29, fuses F29, parts P185 / P186, cavities DP-DCU-D 10, can_fields 0x300/4, the DCU firmware's comment on that byte. Block 02.16's wording ("two A/C sensor wires if the ECU runs the A/C") is now the case.

title: A seventh 6-way plug at the dash post for the optional engine wires
body:
**Add a seventh plug at the dash post: a 6-way DT pair, and leave room for a fifth extra receptacle on the dash post panel now.**

His answer (block 02.16, desktop, 2026-10-13): option (a), "Add a seventh plug, a 6-way DT pair (about $10-20, confirm), and leave room for a fifth receptacle on the dash post panel now. Every option keeps a place, with one spare. Forecloses nothing; costs a little panel room." No words typed.

Reasoning: with every option the leg needs 71 places and six 12-way plugs have 67 usable (D-443's count assumed the two plugs at the post were empty; five cavities are not). A seventh plug gives the airflow meter (LW24), the cam phaser pair (LW34) and the neutral switch pair (LW38) a place, with one spare. The recommendation's flip condition (no panel room for a fifth receptacle when measured) is a measurement for electrical E13, not a reason to hold the ruling.

Consequences: D-443's plug count becomes seven (six 12-way plus one 6-way DT pair); K6's last five conductors can be assigned; electrical E13 leaves room for five extra receptacles at the post (its note already carries this). Price and part number carry `confirm` until sourced.

title: A coolant level switch in the swap's expansion tank with a cluster warning
body:
**Fit a coolant level switch in the swap's expansion tank, wired through L1-S2 11 to the cluster's spare input (IC17), with a low-coolant warning on the cluster screen.**

His answer (block 02.17, desktop, 2026-10-13): option (a), "Fit a coolant level switch in the swap's expansion tank (about $20-40, confirm), wired through L1-S2 11 to the cluster's spare input, with a warning on the screen. Uses the spare input; if the wideband gauge later needs that input as its fallback (electrical B2), the switch moves to an engine-computer input and the warning comes over CAN." No words typed. A discussion rode along in context: his earlier answer in the same session (2026-10-13T09:59:15-06:00) was (b); the final answer, a minute later, is (a), and (a) is the ruling.

Reasoning: the 12A's radiator level sensor (PT292) leaves with the radiator; without a replacement the engine computer's temperature is the only guard, and a leak shows only once hot, on aluminum heads. The cavity already exists, so no new one is needed.

Consequences: the swap uses L1-S2 11 (HO09); coolant level rows are added to ls_devices / ls_wires and a switch to the swap's parts list (DS10) in the plan run; if the wideband gauge takes IC17 (electrical B2) the switch moves to an engine-computer input. Price carries `confirm`.

title: The seventh plug L1-S7 carries the airflow meter, neutral switch and cam phaser conductors; L1-S2 3-5 stay free spares
body:
**The seventh plug is L1-S7, a DT06-6S / DT04-6P pair at the dash post: it carries the airflow meter signal (LW24), the neutral switch pair (LW38) and the cam phaser pair (LW34), with cavity 4 its one spare; the three cavities D-489 freed in L1-S2 (3, 4, 5) stay free as the slow-lines plug's spares.**

Applies D-500 (block 02.16, option (a)) to the cavity plan - K6's last five conductors. No new words from Camden.

Reasoning: D-500 places all three optional functions on the seventh plug, so they go there even though L1-S2 3, 4 and 5 are free since D-489 - three cavities would not hold five conductors, and keeping the optional wires together in one plug lets a speed-density build with no phaser and no neutral switch leave L1-S7 unpinned entirely. Within the plug the two signal-class lines (the airflow meter's frequency signal, the neutral switch and its return) sit at cavities 1 to 3 and the phaser solenoid's 1.5 A slow PWM pair at 5 and 6, the spare at 4 between them - the same separation L1-S4 keeps between coil triggers and the O2 heater drivers. Which of the phaser pair is the driver and which the feed is read off the EMU PRO's output type (K5, confirm). The size-16 contacts, GXL 20 AWG and the seal range are as the other signal plugs (ls_wires.awg).

Consequences: ls_cavities gains L1-S7 1 to 6 and its housing note widens to L1-S7; L1-S2 3, 4 and 5 stay `free` (sealing plugs); the plug pair is a swap parts row priced `confirm` (D-500); HO14 counts seven plugs; electrical E13 leaves room for a fifth extra receptacle on the post panel (D-500, already in its note).

title: The coolant level switch is LD30 / LW49 on L1-S2 11 into IC17, its other terminal grounded in the bay
body:
**The coolant level switch is LD30 in the swap's expansion tank, one crossing conductor LW49 pinned at L1-S2 11 into the ICU's spare input IC17 (DP-ICU-B 9, node N67); its other terminal is grounded in the bay, as the brake fluid switch is.**

Applies D-501 (block 02.17, option (a)) to the device, wire, cavity and parts tables. No new words from Camden.

Reasoning: D-501 names the cavity (L1-S2 11) and the input (IC17); what was left to the plan is the wiring pattern. A two-wire float switch is wired like the reservoir's brake fluid switch (LW41, LD27): one terminal to a bay ground, the signal through the leg to the cluster's input, so it needs one cavity, which D-501 already found. Whether the switch closes or opens on low level is read off the switch bought and set in the ICU's input (confirm, R11); an open circuit must read as a warning, so the preferred switch closes to ground with the float up and opens low - a broken wire then shows as low coolant, not as silence. The ICU input's pull-up is the ICU's own (DP-ICU-B 9 is wired, HO09). If the wideband gauge takes IC17 (electrical B2), LW49's dash end moves to an engine-computer input and the warning comes on CAN (D-501) - the cavity does not change.

Consequences: ls_devices LD30, ls_wires LW49 (crosses 1, signal, 20 AWG GXL), ls_cavities L1-S2 11 pinned to LW49, parts CL01 priced 20-40 confirm (D-501), HO09 updated; the warning on the cluster screen is the ICU's firmware (electrical, the swap's CAN work - K5 lists the ICU inputs the swap uses).

title: The 12A is not rebuilt; it screeched on its first crank after the breakdown, and the LS is its replacement
body:
**The 12A is not rebuilt.** After the breakdown it cranked fast on the Ionic and made a loud metal screech (00-CAR K-025). Camden reads that as a broken apex seal, or a part from the carburettor inside the engine, and rules out rebuilding it. The car's next engine is the LS (D-393).

His words (chat, 2026-10-16): "safe to say the engine in blown. i had 3 psi at the fuel pressure gauge and a small leak at the carb inlet which i fixed, i went to start the car and is instantly cranked witht the new healthy battery but, made the most awful metal screaching noise ever. i can only espect that i broke an apex seal and its griding up in there or the something broke off inside the carb ... i dont want to rebuild that engine, its most likely toast through and through."

**What is known and what is not (R11).** Known: no rebuild. Not known: where the noise comes from. A starter that does not mesh with the flexplate also screeches, and nobody has turned the engine by hand or tested its compression. This ruling does not depend on which it is.

**What follows.** CP01 (the 12A, its automatic, the Weber and the exhaust come out, boxed or sold) stands. Whether the new wiring is first started on the 12A or waits for the LS is electrical's block 01.61, raised the same day; it also settles whether the 12A is sold running or dead. No row changes here.

title: The swap's first design pass: J3, K2, DS04, DS06 done; emissions, rear axle and accessory drive asked; the dead 12A comes out without waiting on the freeze
body:
**The engine swap's first design pass with the 12A gone. Four design rows are done (J3, K2, DS04, DS06). Three choices that spend money are his, as blocks 01.62 (emissions), 01.63 (rear axle) and 01.64 (accessory drive). The FB-specific findings sit on the rows that use them. The dead 12A no longer waits on the freeze to come out. The project moves from PROPOSED to PLANNING.**

His words (chat, 2026-10-16): "please help me dive into the engine swap project ... please adjust the gates as well ... please refactor and do a first pass on engine swap to acueally put some real meat into that project."

**What was found** (web, 2026-10-16; every figure confirm until checked on the part, R11):
- **CD009 (J3).** No published drawing. A builder's eyeballed figures on an uncut unit (HybridZ): about 40 in overall, about 29 in from the bellhousing face to the output, about 27 in to the mount, the shifter hole about 32-34 in back once relocated or shortened. Sikky's adapter (TAK-CD, $1,724.97) keeps the Nissan bellhousing and brings its own flywheel (CDFW-01) and a low-profile starter (SK-02). The 350Z clutch and a Nissan pilot bearing are bought apart; ARP 244-2902 bolts are required.
- **Emissions (K2).** Larimer County is in the program, and a 1982 car is tested every two years. After an engine change, the limits and the equipment checked follow whichever is newest, the vehicle or the engine (Regulation 11, 5 CCR 1001-13, form DR2365). Collector plates waive the test for a 1976-1985 car only if it was so registered before 2009-09-01 and never lapsed. This is block 01.62.
- **Clutch (DS06).** The CD009 keeps its external Nissan slave. A Wilwood compact master on the FB firewall (Sikky's own CD009 kit uses 7/8 in) feeds it through a braided line and a fitting into the Nissan slave. The pedals come from a 1981-85 FB 5-speed box, or are the car's own with a clutch pedal and a longer pivot bolt (RX7Club, an FB owner). Parts CL02-CL06. The start interlock's clutch switch is electrical Y81.
- **Cooling (DS04).** FB V8 builds ran a Howe shelf 342AA (27 x 16.5 x 3 in, front tension-rod brackets removed) or a Granny's Radiator on a custom spreader bar, with a JTR steam vent tee. The fan has its own fuse and relay (electrical D-468). Parts CO01-CO04.
- **FB V8 builds** (LS1Tech, an 1984 FB with an LS3 / T56 / 8.8; RX7Club, an 1985 FB with an LT1 / T5):
  - Mounts: the crossmember drilled to set the engine about 1.5 in back, to clear the balancer from the sway bar (OP51); a custom transmission crossmember, because an automatic FB's mounts differ from a manual's (OP52).
  - Oil pan: an F-body pan, or the pan modified to clear the steering centre link.
  - Headers: made by hand, and they fit only with the starter out.
  - Driveshaft: shortened.
  - Rear axle: a Ford 8.8 with a Watts link.
  - Front: 5-lug with FC or Turbo II hubs.
- **Rear axle (DS08).** Drifting Dad sells weld-on FB 8.8 brackets ($300), a panhard bar ($220) or Watts bars ($300), a complete Ford 9 ($3,500, 6+ months) and a front 5-lug kit for FC hubs ($300). An Explorer 8.8 brings rear discs and 5x4.5 in hubs, so the front and the wheels go 5-lug. This is block 01.63; options OP41, OP43 and OP45.
- **Accessory drive (DS01).** It carries a 160 A or larger alternator (D-457), the water pump and the A/C compressor, and no steering pump (the GS steers manually). The candidates are ICT Billet's compact Corvette-spaced kit (its with-A/C price unread), Holley's 20-138 (about $1,850-2,070, a high mount), or a junkyard F-body or C5 set with an aftermarket alternator. This is block 01.64; options OP70-OP72. The `options.system` enum gains `accessory` (CLAUDE.md §3: widened deliberately).

**Gates.** CP01 (the 12A out) drops DS11 and waits only on DS13 (weigh the front first). The empty bay is what the new Camden row M01 measures, and DS07 now waits on M01. DS01, DS03 and DS08 also wait on their blocks.

**Phase.** PLANNING. The project is the first one now (D-618), and planning has begun in earnest. The freeze (DS11) still moves it to SOURCING.

**Left for the next plan run.** K5 (the ECU's pins at the dash: the EMU PRO's pinout is still not read). J5 (the donor search, run before a yard trip). DS02, DS07 and DS09 wait on M01 and DS13. DS10 (the budget) waits on all of them.

title: Emissions: the LS keeps the donor's converters, O2 sensors and EVAP so it passes as its engine's year
body:
**The LS keeps its donor's whole emissions system: both catalytic converters in the new exhaust, every O2 sensor, the EVAP canister and purge, and PCV, all run by the ECU, so the car passes Colorado's test as a car of the engine's year. Block 01.62, option (a).**

His answer (desktop app, 2026-10-16): choice (a), no words. In chat the same day: "please follow recomendetions on all blocks for the engine project".

The option in full: "(a) Keep the donor's whole emissions system: both catalytic converters in the new exhaust, every O2 sensor, the EVAP canister and purge, PCV. The ECU runs them. Costs the converters (about $200-600 for two direct-fit universal ones, confirm) plus the donor's own sensors and canister, pulled with the engine. Forecloses nothing, and the car registers."

**Why.** After an engine change, Regulation 11 tests the newest of the vehicle and the engine (D-621, K2). The collector exemption is not pursued; it would need collector plates held since before 2009-09-01, and nothing says the car has them.

**In the data.**
- ls_devices LD11 (the upstream O2 sensors) and LD20 (EVAP purge) are no longer optional. Their notes say so; whether LD11's narrowbands or the wideband drive the fuelling is still the ECU's (K5).
- DS03 designs in two converters and the downstream O2 bungs.
- BR02 pulls the donor's O2 sensors, EVAP canister, purge valve and PCV parts with the engine.
- parts EM01 (two converters; whether Colorado requires CARB- or EPA-approved aftermarket units is confirm) and EM02 (the donor's O2 sensors, canister and purge parts).
- TU06 takes the car to a referee station with form DR2365.

title: Rear axle: a yard Explorer 8.8 with discs on Drifting Dad's FB brackets, and the front goes 5-lug
body:
**The LS's rear axle is a yard 1995-2001 Explorer Ford 8.8 with rear discs, on Drifting Dad's weld-on FB brackets with their panhard bar or Watts bars. The front goes 5-lug with their FC-hub kit. Block 01.63, option (a).**

His answer (desktop app, 2026-10-16): choice (a), no words. In chat the same day: "please follow recomendetions on all blocks for the engine project".

The option in full: "(a) A 1995-2001 Explorer Ford 8.8 from a yard, which has rear discs and 31-spline axles, on Drifting Dad's weld-on FB brackets ($300) with their panhard bar ($220) or Watts bars ($300). The front goes 5-lug with their FC-hub kit ($300 plus FC hubs, bearings and brakes). About $1,000-2,000 all in (confirm the axle's price and whether it must be narrowed for the FB's track). title: Donors: only the essentials are pulled - the pull lists - and today's yard search recorded
body:
**From the donors only the essentials are pulled: what the plan reuses and is worth reconditioning. Anything that takes as much effort to restore as buying new, or that the plan already replaces, is left on the car. The pull lists are fixed below. Today's donor search, the first live one since 2026-09-23, is recorded in sightings SG17-SG32.**

His words (chat, 2026-10-16): "i would like to only bull the essentials worth fixing up. parts that are as much efort to fix and resore and make look/function new i will just buy new. the engine/transmission/rearaxle's that i actually find might change things"

**Engine donor (BR02).**
- **Take:** the long block with its intake manifold; the drive-by-wire throttle body and the cab's accelerator pedal (same generation); the fuel rails and injectors; the coils, their brackets and sub-harness; the crank, cam, knock, MAP, coolant and oil-pressure sensors; the engine harness whole (K4 reads the pin letters off it); the O2 sensors, the EVAP canister and purge valve, and the PCV parts (D-622).
- **Read before paying:** the VIN's 8th digit, the odometer, the oil on the dipstick, compression if the yard allows it.
- **Leave:** the accessories (ICT drive, D-624); the truck oil pan (DS02); the exhaust manifolds (custom headers, DS03); the flexplate and torque converter (Sikky flywheel); the ECM (EMU PRO, D-446); the radiator and fans (CO01, CO02); the mounts; the automatic. Gaskets, seals and the timing set are new at the rebuild (RB rows).

**Axle donor (BR07).**
- **Take:** the complete disc-brake rear end: axle shafts, rotors, calipers and brackets, the parking-brake shoes and cable ends, the hard lines on the housing, the diff cover with its tag.
- **Read:** the ratio and the limited-slip from the tag (one wheel spun: the other turns the same way with a limited-slip); the spline count from the shaft if it is out.
- **Leave:** springs, shackles, U-bolts, shocks and the driveshaft.

**CD009 (BR03).** None is in any Front Range U-Pull, so it is bought used and shipped: with its bellhousing, shifter, slave cylinder, release bearing and fork, and the hard line. The clutch is new (CL05).

**What today's search found** (U-Pull-&-Pay's three yards, read through their inventory service; LKQ's two refuse automated reads):
- No L33 anywhere.
- One LM4, at Colorado Springs (SG17).
- Eleven AFM aluminum 5.3s (LC9, LH6), so the AFM delete already planned (RB01) is the likely path.
- Four V8 AWD Explorers and Mountaineers (SG28-SG31).
- No 350Z; one G35 coupe with its gearbox unknown (SG32).

The engine actually bought may change the plan (Gen III or Gen IV, AFM, VVT): ls_wires already covers both generations, and the AFM delete and VVT are rows.

When the donors may be bought is his question, block 01.65.

title: Engine: the junkyard LS trio, restored at home to a remanufacturer's standard and dressed for a clean bay

Block 01.68 (engine source) is answered with a junkyard engine, fully restored at home to the standard of a remanufactured engine:

title: The BP swap's plan system by system - cooling, oil, fuel (return-style), intake, exhaust (one converter), mounts, driveshaft, front drive, clutch, wiring - each turbo-ready where it costs little
body:
**The BP swap's plan, system by system: what is kept, what is made, what is bought, and what is left ready for the turbo. It is the design rows' starting point, frozen by his ruling at DS11.** Every figure is secondary or confirm until Mazda's own manual (BP03) or a measurement on the parts in hand (BD01, CD08) replaces it (R11).

**The engine (00-CAR specs, not fitted).**
- 1.8 L DOHC 16-valve inline-four: iron block, aluminum head, 83 x 85 mm, 9.0:1.
- 128 hp and 110 lb-ft in 1994-95, 133 hp and 114 lb-ft in 1996-97 (US ratings).
- Timing belt with hydraulic lash adjusters.
- Oil about 3.8 qt, or 4.0 qt with the filter. Coolant about 6.3 qt.
- At about 5,000 ft it makes roughly 15% less, about 105-115 hp at the wheels.

The gearbox: 5-speed, 3.136 / 1.888 / 1.330 / 1.000 / 0.814, about 2.1 qt of GL-4 gear oil (S-611). The car is an automatic today, so it needs a clutch pedal, a master cylinder and a line to the Miata's slave (DS06's rows carry over).

**Turbo-ready, rule for every system.** Do it now only if it is cheap, and only because doing it later would mean taking the engine out or undoing a finished job. Buy no boost parts.

**Cooling (BP07).**
- An aluminum radiator in the FB's support, sized for the turbo stage so it is bought once.
- Hose necks matched to the BP. One electric puller fan on its own relay and fuse (D-468, HO02).
- Heater hoses to the FB's heater core. An expansion tank with the level switch (D-501, D-507).
- A new thermostat and hoses.
- The BP's known hot No. 4 cylinder: the rear-outlet coolant reroute is offered as an option at BP07 (about $150-250), because doing it later re-plumbs the upper hose.
- Turbo-ready: the radiator's size, and a capped coolant tap for a water-cooled turbo if the reroute housing has one.

**Oil (DS02).**
- The BP's own wet sump, pan and pickup, checked against the FB's crossmember and steering linkage in CAD.
- The filter's access is checked against the frame rail; a filter relocation only if it is blocked.
- Oil-pressure sensor to the ECU, and the PMU's fuel-pump gate (HO04).
- Turbo-ready: a tee at the pressure-sender port with a plugged feed outlet (about $20-50). A -10 return bung welded into the pan above the oil level while the pan is off for its gasket (about $15-30; the welder is rented anyway), plugged.
- No dry sump: it adds the most plumbing of anything on the engine, and a street FB does not need it.

**Fuel (BP08, supersedes D-448).**
- The Phantom 340 in the tank stays (D-447; already big enough for a turbo).
- The rail returns to a return-style system: the BP's own rail and its manifold-referenced regulator (boost-referenced once there is boost), and the FB's existing steel return pipe (00-CAR PT177).
- The 58 psi filter-regulator by the tank is no longer needed.
- The carburettor-era return check valve (PT120) is checked for restriction or removed.
- New EFI-rated hose from the frame lines to the rail, a filter, and the O5 soft fuse as planned (HO12).
- Turbo-ready: the regulator and the pump. Only the injectors change later.

**Intake (DR04).**
- A filter in a cold-air box fed from outside air, away from the radiator and the manifold.
- A tube to the BP's throttle body, with an IAT sensor boss and the PCV fresh-air port.
- The vane airflow meter is deleted; the EMU PRO runs speed-density on MAP.
- The idle valve is kept. The throttle cable from the FB's pedal is fitted to the BP's throttle body.
- Turbo-ready: the filter box's position is chosen so that later the turbo's inlet takes it, and the tube becomes the charge pipe's last length.

**Exhaust (DS03, supersedes D-622's two-converter LS layout; the rule is unchanged).**
- The BP's own manifold (kept, if it clears the steering box in CAD), then a downpipe with a flex section.
- Then one converter with the upstream and downstream O2 sensors, then 2.5 in pipe to one muffler.
- EVAP canister and purge, and PCV, kept and run by the ECU. The car is tested as a car of the engine's year (D-622's rule; BP02 confirms how a JDM BP is tested).
- Turbo-ready: everything after the downpipe joint is reused, and the converter is sized for the turbo's flow.

**Mounts (DS07).**
- The BP's own side brackets on the block. Fabricated adapter plates to the FB crossmember's mount positions, on rubber mounts.
- The engine sits as far back and low as the clearance proof allows, to keep the FB's balance.
- The gearbox is held by a fabricated crossmember from the gearbox's PPF bosses to the FB's transmission-mount points. The Miata's PPF itself does not fit the FB's axle.
- The shifter's position against the FB's tunnel opening is J4.
- Turbo-ready: nothing sits where the turbo and downpipe will go.

**Driveshaft (BP09).**
- Made to length by a driveshaft shop once the mock-up gives the measured length.
- The front is a slip yoke on the Miata gearbox's output spline (from a yard Miata's shaft, J6). The rear is a flange to the FB's companion flange (00-CAR PT435). It is balanced.
- Turbo-ready: a tube and joints rated above the turbo's torque.

**Front drive and alternator (BP04).**
- The Miata's alternator and water-pump drive stay.
- The power-steering pump and its belt go: the FB's box is manual.
- The A/C compressor stays on its bracket with its belt; its hoses, condenser and charge come with the luxury stage (D-489 still holds at that stage).
- The alternator's rating is block 01.71. The 163 A target (D-457) cannot be met by a bolt-in BP alternator.

**Clutch (BP10).**
- The FB manual pedal box and master (CL02, CL03), and a line to the Miata's slave.
- A Miata 1.8 clutch kit with a pilot and release bearing, and the flywheel resurfaced.
- Turbo-ready: a clutch rated above the turbo's torque, if it costs little more than stock.

**The engine wiring leg (BP05, then K5).**
- The BP's devices replace the LS's: 4 injectors, the coil pack (and its igniter if that year needs one), the cam and crank sensors of its year, the idle valve, TPS, coolant sensor, a new IAT, MAP, the O2 sensors, purge, oil pressure, the alternator, the starter, and the reverse and neutral switches.
- Road speed comes from the gearbox's speedometer drive (electrical Y82).
- The crank interlock is the clutch pedal switch (electrical Y81).
- Turbo-ready: the boost-control solenoid output, a second IAT and an oil-temperature input are wired and plugged now.

**Supersedes:**
- D-448 (returnless 58 psi).
- D-622 (the LS emissions layout; the BP keeps the same rule).
- D-623 (the Explorer 8.8 and 5-lug front, now the turbo stage's; the FB axle stays, since the BP makes about the 12A's torque).
- D-624 (ICT's LS front drive).

The parts table, options, specs and work rows are changed in the same pass. The budget stays a query over parts (DS10), never a typed total.

title: The engine project is worked in zones - bp, oil, trans, fuel (tank, pump, lines), radiator (hoses), intake, exhaust, mounts, wiring - a zones table, a zone on every work and parts row, one folder per zone
body:
**The engine project is worked in zones: a zones table, a zone column on work and parts, and one folder per zone under 02-PROJECTS/01-engine holding that zone's cad/ and its files. The zones are bp (with bp/oil), trans, fuel (fuel/tank, fuel/pump, fuel/lines), radiator (with radiator/hoses), intake, exhaust, mounts and wiring.**

His words, 2026-10-17, in chat: "plese separate the engine project into its areas so we can work on zones there is fouders for my suggestions of the split"

**His folders.** He made bp/, trans/, fuel/tank, fuel/pump, fuel/lines, radiator/ and radiator/hoses, each with cad/ and data/. Each becomes a zones row with its folder as its id.

**The zones he had no folder for.** The systems D-630 plans are added: intake, exhaust, mounts and wiring, and bp/oil inside the engine. Their folders are made the same way. A .gitkeep keeps each folder in git, so it reaches the other clones.

**Reading taken.** A zone is not a separate area. rx7.py finds an area only at ROOT/<area> or 02-PROJECTS/<project> (CLAUDE.md section 1). Splitting the project's tables into one record per folder would break the gates across them and the one home per fact (R2).

So the record stays the project's one set of tables, and each row names its zone. A zone's data/ folder holds the files that are not the record: measurements as photos, vendor sheets, drawings. Its cad/ holds its models.

This is small (section 3): only rows change, and it can be undone by editing rows. If he meant one separate record per zone, that is a tool change for 02-APP and a new block.

The old top-level cad/ folder keeps the LS reference models (D-625).

title: BP alternator: the FD RX-7's 100 A now on the BP's bracket, 160 A at the luxury/turbo stage
body:
**The BP runs the FD RX-7's 100 A alternator on the BP's own bracket for the engine-stage car; the 160 A unit on a custom bracket comes with the luxury and turbo stage.** Block 01.71 answered (a).

His answer, option (a) in full: "The FD RX-7 100 A alternator now, on the BP's own bracket, about $100-250 used or rebuilt. Enough for the engine-stage car. A 160 A unit on a custom bracket comes with the luxury and turbo stage, when the luxury loads arrive. Forecloses nothing; the 100 A unit is sold or kept as a spare then." He typed no further words.

Reasoning: no bolt-in unit above about 100-110 A exists for the BP (S-613); until the luxury loads go in the load is the engine, the pump (about 12.2 A, V-040), one fan and the basics, which 100 A covers. The recommendation's flip condition (luxury comfort loads before the turbo stage) is not met by anything in the record today.

D-457 is not superseded: its 160 A floor stands for the full luxury load (about 163 A) and is met at the luxury/turbo stage, not on day one. D-630's open point (the alternator's rating) is settled for the engine stage.

Consequences: AC02 is the FD RX-7 100 A on the BP's bracket now; BP04 designs the front drive around it; K7 caps charge current for the 100 A unit now and is revisited at 160 A when the luxury stage arrives.

title: The BP must pass emissions as its engine's year (BP02)
body:
**The BP swap must pass Colorado emissions tested as the engine's year (1994-97 Miata BP); BP02 is closed on that rule. How the referee sets a JDM engine's year, tailpipe versus OBD, and whether the EMU PRO passes were not answered and are not assumed.**

His words on work BP02 (done): "Must pass for the year of the engine".

Reading (§3, keeps most options open): this fixes the requirement D-630 already assumed - the car is held to the engine's year and must pass - not a report of the call to the referee. It rules out any plan that only works if the car is tested as a 1982. It does not say a test method or that an aftermarket ECU is accepted, so no plan may rely on either until a referee or the first test says so; the BP exhaust keeps its converter and O2 sensors, and the ECU choice stays open.

Consequences: BP02 done with the rule as its result. Nothing is bought on the strength of an ECU passing. Any later finding that the BP cannot pass is a contradiction and a block.

title: DR01: every BP and 5-speed part ruled keep, delete, replace, provision or check (bp_items BI01-BI42); the M/T throttle sensor is an idle switch and is replaced by a linear one
body:
**DR01 done: every part on the BP and its 5-speed is ruled in bp_items (BI01-BI42) - keep, delete, replace, provision for luxury or the turbo, or check on the engine in hand.**

**Findings the plan did not have (S-623, the 1994 sections):**
- The manual-gearbox throttle position sensor is an idle switch only (terminals E and IDL), and the EMU PRO needs a linear one. The Miata automatic's TP sensor or an NB one on an adapter replaces it: parts AI02.
- The vane airflow meter carries the intake air temperature sensor, so deleting the meter needs a separate IAT in the intake tube: parts AI03.
- The 1994 BP has a coolant-to-oil cooler at the filter, which is kept.
- The 1994 tests list EGR codes, but the 1994 vacuum diagram has no EGR. It is ruled check: if the engine in hand has EGR, it is kept for the emissions test (BP02).
- The pressure regulator control solenoid (a hot-restart aid) is deleted; the regulator's line goes straight to the manifold.
- The cam angle sensor on the intake cam is the trigger. A 1996-97 engine adds a crank sensor (BP01 asks the year).

**Provisions:** the power-steering pump, bracket and belt (luxury's power steering, D-636); the A/C compressor (luxury's A/C).

**Replaced:** the alternator (the FD 100 A, D-633), the oil-pressure switch (a sensor on a tee with the plugged turbo feed), the intake (DR04), the PPF (a fabricated crossmember, DS07), and the clutch (renewed).

Every figure and fit is confirm until BD01, BD06 and BD15 on the parts in hand (R11).

title: The FB side of the swap ruled part by part: fb_items, 337 parts out, kept, modified or checked by a named row
body:
**The FB side of the swap is ruled part by part in fb_items: every 00-CAR part of the engine, transmission, driveline, fuel, ignition and cooling - 337 parts.**

- **Out (275):** the 12A and everything on it, the automatic and its selector, the propeller shaft, the carburettor and air cleaner equipment, the external fuel pump and regulator, the 12A's ignition, radiator, fan and pump, the old exhaust.
- **Keep (32):** the rear axle and differential (the 8.8 is the turbo stage's), the companion flange the new shaft bolts to, the tank's fittings, the accelerator pedal.
- **Modify (2):** the tank (its top cut for the Phantom 340) and its hoses.
- **Check (28):** decided by the row named in each:
  - DS07: the engine and transmission mounts.
  - DS03: the heat shields and hangers.
  - BP08: the steel fuel pipes, the return check valve and EVAP.
  - BP07: the sub tank, level sensor and shroud.
  - DR04: the throttle cable.
  - J4 and CP03: the shift-lever boot and floor seal.

The rules are by part name (the 12A's and the automatic's parts out; the named exceptions checked). A wrong ruling is fixed in the row. The FB's electrical parts in the bay stay 02-electrical's.

title: The 12A stays in until the BP is ready, the design frozen and the parts in hand; the bay is measured around it (M01) and re-checked the day it comes out (M02)
body:
**The 12A stays in the car as long as possible. It comes out (CP01) only when three things are true: the BP is serviced and assembled on its stand (DB01), the design is frozen (DS11) and the car-prep parts are in hand (BR06). The bay is measured around the 12A (M01, now gated on nothing), and what it hides is re-measured the day it comes out (M02, which CD08 now waits on).**

His words, 2026-10-17, in chat: "id also prefer to leave the 12a in as long as possible for changes in the plan"

**Why it works:**
- The 12A is small, so the crossmember, mount pads, rails, steering box, firewall and tunnel can all be measured from above and below with it in place.
- Only the floor between the rails and the tunnel mouth stay hidden, and M02 takes those the day it comes out, before any cutting (CP03 and CP04 wait on CD08).
- The car runs and can be driven until the swap is ready to go in, and every design choice stays open that long.

**Changes:** M01's gate was CP01 and is now empty; CP01's gate was DS13 and is now DS13 DS11 DB01 BR06; CD08 adds M02; M02 is new.
